title: Graphic
coreIdea: Reduce the street to pure formal elements — shape, line, contrast, color block, geometry — so the picture works primarily through visual structure.
whyItMatters: Formal strength is the foundation underneath narrative. A picture with strong graphic bones can carry weak content; a picture with interesting content but weak formal structure usually fails. This day isolates the formal skill so you can see it clearly.
shootingBrief: Bold graphic opportunities: high-contrast shapes, strong diagonals, color fields, repeating geometry, silhouettes against plain backgrounds. The picture should hold even if the content is not immediately recognizable. Minimum 8 frames that succeed primarily on formal terms. Volume 40–70. Black-and-white thinking helps even if you shoot color.
technicalFocus: Settings: Careful exposure for contrast. Protect highlights if you want deep blacks.
Focusing: On the key graphic plane.
Stance: Precise framing and edge control are essential.
Light: Hard light or strong color contrast preferred.
Distance: Variable — choose what best isolates the graphic structure.
Content can be minimal.
failureModes: Weak formal structure dressed up as “graphic.”
Busy frames that lack a clear dominant shape, line, or contrast.
Accepting content interest as a substitute for formal strength.
Poor edge control.

goodVsExcellent.good: Strong shapes or lines are present.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The formal arrangement is so clear and resolved that the picture holds power even if the subject is not immediately identifiable. Structure is the subject.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Analyses of Cartier-Bresson geometry.
Contemporary pure graphic street work.
Formal composition breakdowns in street contexts.
Cartier-Bresson’s strongest geometric frames. Certain Leiter and Meyerowitz formal color work. High-contrast contemporary graphic street.

title: Children
coreIdea: Photograph children in public space with genuine interest in their world, strict dignity, and clear ethical limits.
whyItMatters: Children are a high-stakes subject. Doing this well builds emotional intelligence, timing for unpredictable movement, lower-angle seeing, and personal ethical boundaries that apply to all street portraiture. It forces you to decide in real time what is acceptable and what is not.
shootingBrief: Children playing, walking with adults, or occupying public space in interesting ways. Prefer wider context and interactions over tight facial close-ups of strangers’ children. Minimum 6 frames. If a parent notices and shows discomfort, move on immediately. Volume 40–60.
technicalFocus: Settings: Fast shutter (often 1/500s or higher), AF-C with tracking.
Focusing: Continuous on the child.
Stance: Lower angles frequently work better and feel less predatory.
Light: Available light. Avoid harsh overhead sun that creates ugly shadows on faces.
Distance: Respectful. Wider context is both safer and often stronger.
Primarily candid. Approached only with clear parental comfort and only if it serves a stronger picture.
failureModes: Exploitative or cute framing.
Tight faces of strangers’ children without meaningful context.
Ignoring parental signals.
Making the child look vulnerable or performed for the camera.

goodVsExcellent.good: A decent, non-exploitative picture of a child.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The frame shows the child’s world or energy with dignity and the same formal strength you would demand of any adult subject. Ethics and craft are both visible.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Vivian Maier analyses that include her child and lower-angle work.
Practical discussions of ethics when photographing children in public.
Timing and movement with unpredictable subjects.
Vivian Maier’s stronger child frames. Erwitt’s more playful child and family work. Clear personal rules from working photographers who photograph families and children in public spaces.

title: Projects
coreIdea: Work one narrow idea, place, or theme for the entire session so the pictures begin to form a coherent set.
whyItMatters: Isolated exercises produce isolated pictures. Projects create coherence, deeper seeing, and the possibility of a real body of work. This day is the bridge from practice exercises to self-directed photography. Most lasting street work is project-based.
shootingBrief: Choose one narrow constraint (a single block, a type of storefront, people carrying specific things, a particular light condition, a recurring gesture, one intersection, one kind of interaction). Shoot only inside that constraint. Aim for a coherent set of 8–12 frames that could start a longer project. Write a one-sentence project statement in your notes. Volume 40–70.
technicalFocus: Settings: Keep approach and look consistent across the set.
Focusing, stance, light, distance: Whatever the project demands, held consistent so the pictures sit together.
Consistency of method strengthens the set more than variety.
Mix of candid and any approached portraits that fit the project idea.
failureModes: Project idea too broad to create coherence.
Inconsistent approach so the set does not hold together.
Abandoning the constraint when the street offers something tempting outside it.
Ending with a pile of related but not coherent pictures.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The set has internal consistency of seeing, light, and approach. The strongest frames could continue as a real body of work and the project statement is clear and true.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Joel Meyerowitz on sustained observation and developing identity through work.
Working photographers discussing long-term street projects.
Editing and sequencing short project sets.
Sustained projects by the reference photographers (Meyerowitz’s larger bodies of work, Winogrand’s major series, contemporary project-based workers such as Gustavo Minas and Phil Penman).

title: Vertical / Horizontal
coreIdea: Make orientation an active decision rather than a camera default. Shoot half the session only vertical, half only horizontal, and compare.
whyItMatters: Default horizontal is lazy. Orientation changes emphasis, meaning, and the relationships inside the frame. Vertical often isolates and stacks; horizontal often relates and contextualizes. Making the choice deliberate improves every frame you take afterward.
shootingBrief: First half of the session: only vertical (portrait orientation). Second half: only horizontal (landscape orientation). Revisit the same scenes in both orientations when possible and compare. Minimum 6 strong frames in each orientation. Volume 50–80.
technicalFocus: Settings: Standard street settings for the conditions.
Focusing and light: Unchanged by orientation.
Stance: Recompose fully for the new orientation. Do not simply rotate the camera and crop later.
Distance: Adjust as needed for the new frame shape.
Both candid street and any street portraits.
failureModes: Simply rotating the camera without rethinking the composition.
Weak verticals that are just cropped horizontals.
Ignoring how orientation changes the weight of elements.
Defaulting back to horizontal the moment the exercise feels restrictive.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: Certain scenes clearly belong to one orientation, and you can articulate exactly why. Orientation has become a deliberate compositional tool.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Practical demonstrations of orientation decisions in street work.
Analyses of how masters use vertical versus horizontal for the same subject matter.
Composition discussions that isolate frame shape.
Compare vertical and horizontal frames by Cartier-Bresson, Winogrand, and Meyerowitz of similar subject matter. Notice how the choice changes meaning.

title: Ethics
coreIdea: Shoot with a clear, personal, practical code. Make pictures you would be prepared to show the subjects or defend without rationalization.
whyItMatters: Technical skill without ethical clarity produces work that eventually feels extractive or hollow. This day forces the code into practice under real conditions rather than leaving it as abstract principle. It is the final filter for all the previous days.
shootingBrief: Normal street work with heightened awareness of consent signals, dignity, power dynamics, and potential harm. Actively avoid situations that feel extractive or voyeuristic. If someone notices and shows discomfort, stop, delete if requested, or engage respectfully. Make at least 6 frames you would be willing to show the subjects themselves. Volume 40–60.
technicalFocus: No special technical settings. The constraint is behavioral and ethical.
For approached street portraits: clear, brief, respectful communication.
For candid work: continuous reading of the situation. Distance and stance should never feel predatory.
Your body language and speed of movement communicate as much as the camera.
failureModes: Abstract principles that disappear the moment a strong picture appears.
Rationalizing after the fact (“they didn’t see me,” “it’s public,” “the picture is good enough to justify it”).
Ignoring clear discomfort.
Treating ethics as a one-day exercise instead of a permanent operating system.

goodVsExcellent.good: No obvious ethical breaches in the day’s work.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The pictures are strong and you have a clear, personal rule set that you actually follow under pressure. You know exactly what you will and will not do, and the work reflects that clarity.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Matt Stuart on manners and presence.
Maciej Dakowicz on not being afraid while remaining human.
Plain discussions by working photographers about lines they will not cross and how they handle confrontation.

Personal codes articulated by long-working street photographers. The difference between energetic presence (Winogrand, Meyerowitz) and extractive approaches. Your own previous keepers reviewed against today’s standard.
closingNote: Build the habit of asking the right questions every time you raise the camera.
